lessons.title: Common False Recovery Signals and How to Avoid Them

body.text: Every genuine recovery signal covered so far has a decoy version that can look identical on the surface. This lesson closes Chapter 4 by cataloguing the four false-recovery patterns most likely to fool someone using this exact framework.

children.text: This lesson is deliberately the last one in Chapter 4, because every false signal it covers is a distorted version of a real signal covered earlier in this course. Recognising the genuine article, from Lessons 4.1 through 4.3, is only half the skill. Recognising its impostor is the other half, and it is the half most often skipped.

Lesson 1.3 covered this in the context of India's FY22 GDP print, roughly 9% growth that looked like a boom but, once indexed to the pre-Covid FY20 level, represented barely more than catching back up to where the economy already stood two years earlier. The same trap applies specifically to recovery calls: a strong year-on-year growth, IIP, or earnings print immediately following a depressed base period will always look impressive, whether or not the underlying trend has genuinely accelerated. The check is the same one from Lesson 1.3: look at the indexed level, and where possible the seasonally adjusted quarter-on-quarter momentum, before believing a single YoY number.
False Signal 2: The Inventory Restocking Bump

markDefs.definition: A pattern where small shifts in actual end-consumer demand get amplified into much larger swings in orders and production further up the supply chain, because each link in the chain adjusts its own inventory buffer on top of reacting to the demand shift itself.

children.text: During a slowdown, businesses typically run down existing inventory rather than cut new orders as sharply as falling sales alone would suggest. Once inventories are depleted enough, even flat end-consumer demand can trigger a genuine burst of new orders and production, purely to restock back to normal levels, temporarily lifting PMI and IIP without any real acceleration in underlying demand. This is the classic

from supply chain economics, and it produces a PMI or IIP pop that looks identical to genuine early-cycle recovery on the surface. The check is to look past output and orders to actual end-demand proxies, GST collections growth, retail sales data, or personal consumption expenditure, to see whether consumers or end-users are genuinely buying more, or whether the supply chain is simply refilling itself.
False Signal 3: Fiscal and One-Off Stimulus Masking the Trend

Front-loaded government capex, a pre-election spending push, or a one-off subsidy or tax cut can all produce a genuine, real growth bump for a quarter or two, without reflecting a durable change in the private-sector economy this course's framework is actually trying to read. This is not base-effect distortion, the growth is real, but its source matters. The check here is to separate government spending and one-off measures from private capex and private consumption in the underlying data: a recovery led entirely by public spending, with private investment and consumption still flat, is a fragile one that risks reversing once the fiscal support fades, unlike a recovery where private-sector activity is independently accelerating too.
False Signal 4: The Narrow, Liquidity-Driven Market Rally

Lesson 4.2 covered how a genuinely domestic recovery tends to be led by Financials, Auto, and Real Estate, with IT lagging. A rally driven mainly by global liquidity chasing risk-on sentiment, rather than an improving domestic outlook, can push index levels up in a way that superficially resembles early-cycle recovery, while failing the breadth and sector-leadership checks from that lesson. This matters because a liquidity-driven rally can reverse quickly if global conditions shift, in a way a genuine domestically-led recovery, grounded in the credit cycle and real-economy data from Chapter 3, is less likely to.

body.caption: The four false recovery signals, and the check that catches each one

cells: A strong YoY growth print right after a depressed base period
Check the indexed level and seasonally adjusted QoQ momentum, not just YoY %
A temporary pop in PMI/IIP output and orders
Check end-demand proxies, GST collections, retail sales, personal consumption, separately
Real growth concentrated around a government spending push or a one-off measure
Separate government spending and one-off items from private capex and consumption
A market rally that fails Lesson 4.2's sector-breadth and leadership checks
Check sector leadership composition, especially whether IT is leading instead of lagging

body.text: These four false signals are not mutually exclusive, and real episodes often combine more than one at once, for example a base-effect-flattered growth print that is also partly fiscal-spending-driven. Run through all four checks, not just the first one that seems to explain the data.

body.title: The Chapter 4 Master Verification Checklist
steps: Base effect: check the indexed level and QoQ momentum, not just the YoY growth print
Inventory bump: check GST collections, retail sales, or consumption data to confirm end-demand is genuinely accelerating, not just supply chain restocking
Fiscal distortion: separate government and one-off spending from private capex and consumption trends
Market breadth: check sector leadership against Lesson 4.2's expected sequence, and whether IT is lagging as expected in a domestic recovery
Credit cycle: confirm the credit cycle turn markers from Lesson 4.3, declining NPAs, normalising credit cost, broadening into project finance, are actually present, not just assumed

body.title: Spot the Combined False Signal
body.scenario: GDP growth for the latest quarter is reported at 8.5%, a year after a quarter that had grown only 1.2%. Government capital expenditure was unusually front-loaded this quarter, running well ahead of its full-year budgeted pace. IIP growth of 6% was driven mainly by a jump in the Infrastructure/Construction Goods category. Meanwhile, GST collections growth has been flat at around 5%, roughly matching nominal GDP trend, and private capex announcements tracked by industry bodies have not picked up.
body.prompt: Which of this lesson's false recovery signals, or combination of them, best explains this data? What would you want to see before treating this as a genuine, durable recovery?
body.modelAnswer: This looks like a combination of the base-effect illusion and fiscal/one-off stimulus, reinforcing each other. The 8.5% print follows a depressed 1.2% base, so part of the number is mechanical catch-up rather than fresh acceleration, exactly Lesson 1.3's warning. On top of that, the IIP strength is concentrated in Infrastructure/Construction goods, and government capex was explicitly front-loaded this quarter, pointing to a public-spending-driven bump rather than a private-sector-led recovery. The strongest disconfirming evidence is that GST collections, a genuine end-demand proxy, are only growing in line with nominal GDP trend, not accelerating, and private capex announcements have not picked up either. Before treating this as a genuine, durable recovery, you would want to see private capex and consumption data start accelerating independently of the government spending push, and you would want to see growth sustain over the following one or two quarters after the fiscal front-loading naturally tapers off.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: What specifically distinguishes an inventory restocking bump from a genuine early-cycle demand recovery?
options: An inventory restocking bump only affects the services sector, never manufacturing
In a restocking bump, output and new orders rise to refill depleted inventory even though end-consumer demand, visible in proxies like GST collections or retail sales, has not genuinely accelerated
An inventory restocking bump always lasts longer than a genuine recovery
There is no meaningful difference; both should be treated identically
body.explanation: A restocking bump is a real but temporary supply-chain phenomenon: businesses rebuild depleted inventory even without a genuine pickup in what end-consumers are actually buying. Checking end-demand proxies separately from output and orders data is what distinguishes it from a genuine, demand-led recovery.

body.text: This lesson presents a general, educational framework for identifying false recovery signals. Scenario figures are illustrative, not real reported data. Nothing here is investment advice or a specific market or economic forecast.

points: Base-effect illusions, inventory restocking bumps, fiscal/one-off stimulus, and narrow liquidity-driven rallies are the four false recovery patterns most likely to fool this course's own framework

Each false signal has a specific check: indexed levels for base effects, end-demand proxies for restocking, private-versus-public spending for fiscal distortion, and sector breadth for liquidity-driven rallies
These false signals are not mutually exclusive and often combine, which is why the master checklist runs through all of them rather than stopping at the first plausible explanation
This closes Chapter 4: genuine recovery identification means confirming leading signals, checking sector rotation and credit cycle markers, and actively ruling out each of these four decoys
Chapter 5 applies everything from this course to portfolio positioning by cycle phase, and to detailed historical case studies: the 2008 GFC, the 2020 Covid crash, and the 2013 taper tantrum
